sections.h2: Who bills and who values property tax in Stark County, Ohio?
sections.html:
Two elected offices split the work. The Stark County Auditor values every parcel and runs the exemption programs, and the Stark County Treasurer sends the bills and takes payment. Both are in Canton and both post weekday hours of 8:30 a.m. to 4:30 p.m., closed on government holidays.

The county seat is Canton, and the 374,853 residents counted in 2020 make Stark the eighth most populous county in Ohio. Its parcels fall into seventeen public school districts, from Canton City and Massillon City to Plain Local and Tuslaw Local, and the Treasurer's FAQ says most property tax dollars go to the schools in the owner's district. A tax rate table for each district is available in print at the Treasurer's office.

sections.h2: What are the Stark County tax payment dates and late rules?
sections.html:
Stark County bills in two halves. According to the Treasurer's FAQ, statements go out in January for a February deadline and again in June for July. The newspaper notice of the exact day runs about ten days ahead, and the day can shift: in 2026 the Treasurer's site blamed House Bill 186 for delays that moved the autopay letters from September to October.

  • The county gives no personal extensions. A bill turns late the morning after its stated due date.
  • Mailed payments count by the Postal Service postmark. A private meter stamp does not count, and a check dated after the deadline is treated as late.
  • Late current taxes pick up a ten percent penalty, per the FAQ, and balances left a full year gather interest.
  • A missing bill changes nothing. Download one from the Treasurer's website, ask for an emailed copy at 330-451-7814, or come to the counter.

The Treasurer's site also lists a monthly autopay program, which let enrolled owners spread a year's taxes over scheduled draws. Homeowners whose lender pays from escrow still get a courtesy copy each January. If the lender holds the wrong address after a refinance, the lender itself must ask the Treasurer in writing to fix it.

sections.h2: What does the Treasurer do about long-unpaid Stark County taxes?
sections.html:
Two tools are named in the FAQ. A tax lien certificate sale leaves title with the owner but lets the certificate buyer start a foreclosure if the lien stays open. A tax foreclosure, filed through the Prosecutor, ends in a public Sheriff's sale that does transfer title. The Treasurer's homepage announced a 2026 lien sale, saying that once letters go out only full payment in certified funds removes a parcel, along with a $200 lien fee.

The delinquent tax page lays out the court sequence. After the complaint reaches the Clerk of Courts, a certified-mail summons gives the owner 28 days to answer. An order of sale then moves to the Sheriff, and a newspaper runs the sale notice for three consecutive weeks. Redemption stays open until the court enters its confirmation, and it requires every tax, assessment, penalty, interest charge, fee and court cost, paid in certified funds.

A seller in this position has a known deadline: paying the full balance before the confirmation entry is how an owner redeems the parcel, whether the money comes from savings or from a sale.

sections.h2: Does Stark County offer a back-tax payment plan?
sections.html:
Yes, for delinquent balances only. The Treasurer sets these conditions on its delinquent tax page:

  • The signer must be the titled owner or a documented agent.
  • The delinquent balance has to be at least $1,000. A balance from $1,000 to $1,999 runs 12 months, and $2,000 or more runs 24 months.
  • At signing the owner pays 20 percent of the balance plus the current half.
  • Monthly installments fall on the 20th.
  • An owner who defaulted on an earlier contract cannot sign another.

The current year's bill must still be paid in full on time, and the page says the office cannot extend a due date or plan for current taxes. Any missed payment defaults the contract. Because a plan is a continuing obligation, a seller should ask the Treasurer for the payoff and settle it at closing.

sections.h2: How do I contest a Stark County valuation?
sections.html: File a Board of Revision complaint with the Auditor by the March 31 deadline in ORC 5715.19, or by the close of first-half collection if that is later. Keep paying what you believe is due, since the Treasurer may accept the amount figured on your claimed value. The board has 180 days to rule. The state tax department says some counties run an informal review first, so ask the Stark appraisal department at 330-451-7085 whether that is available. Value is reset by a full reappraisal every six years and an update every three, so a parcel's schedule matters.

sections.h2: Which property tax breaks can a Stark County owner claim?
sections.html:
The Auditor's relief page lists homestead and owner occupancy, the Board of Revision complaint, CAUV for working farmland and exemption or special assessment matters. For tax year 2026 the Ohio Department of Taxation lists the senior and disabled homestead reduction at $29,700 of market value, with an application due December 31 of the year sought. A denial can be taken to the Board of Revision on form DTE 106B within 60 days.

House Bill 96 of 2025 also lets county commissioners add a local-option homestead exemption. The Homestead department at 330-451-7323 can say whether Stark County has adopted one.

sections.h2: What should a Stark County seller check on the tax side before closing?
sections.html:
Ask the Treasurer for the balance on each half, and have the title company confirm the payoff. At the Auditor, the conveyance charge is printed as $.004 of the price rounded up to the next hundred dollars plus fifty cents per tax parcel, paid by check or cash, and the Auditor's stamp must be on the deed before it can be recorded.

The Treasurer's site offers real estate search, prior-year search, the delinquent taxpayer list and a page for Sheriff sales. The delinquent list on the delinquent tax page was posted as of May 1, 2026. Stark County's settlement history helps explain the parcel map: the first permanent settlement came in 1805 at Canton, and the county, named for a Revolutionary War general, was created in 1808.

faqs.q: What is the penalty for paying Stark County property tax late?
faqs.a: Ten percent of the current tax, according to the Treasurer's FAQ. Interest also builds on balances that sit a full year. The county grants no individual extensions.

faqs.q: When do Stark County property tax bills go out?
faqs.a: January mailings serve the February payment, and June mailings serve July. Exact dates run in the Canton Repository shortly before each deadline and can move from year to year.

faqs.q: Can I set up a payment plan for Stark County back taxes?
faqs.a: Yes, but only for delinquent balances of $1,000 or more, and only for the titled owner who has not defaulted before. Expect 20 percent down plus the current half at signing, then payments on the 20th. Current-year tax is excluded.

faqs.q: Where do I file a Stark County property value complaint?
faqs.a: At the Stark County Auditor's office, which passes it to the Board of Revision. The board's lines are 330-451-7998 and 330-451-7949, and the state window closes at the end of March the following year.

faqs.q: Does a Stark County tax foreclosure take my house right away?
faqs.a: No. Several steps come first: a court complaint, a 28-day answer period, an order of sale and three weeks of advertising. The owner can still redeem before the court confirms the sale, using certified funds.
